---
title: "Assembling reports into one document"
---

```{r, include = FALSE}
# A chunk's code sits under "Show code": open when it is what the page is
# about (`fold = "open"`), closed when it only supports it (`fold = "closed"`,
# the default unless the page sets another); `fold = FALSE` shows it plain,
# and so is code of three lines or fewer.
# Its results stay outside, always shown.
.fold_src <- knitr::knit_hooks$get("source")
knitr::knit_hooks$set(source = function(x, options) {
  f <- if (is.null(options$fold)) "closed" else options$fold
  # short code -- three lines or fewer, a chunk or the part of one before
  # its next output -- is shown as it is: folded, it would hide less than
  # the fold itself takes
  if (isFALSE(f) || length(unlist(strsplit(x, "\n", fixed = TRUE))) <= 3L) {
    return(.fold_src(x, options))
  }
  paste0("\n\n<details", if (identical(f, "open")) " open", ">",
         "<summary>Show code</summary>\n\n",
         .fold_src(x, options), "\n\n</details>\n\n")
})
knitr::opts_chunk$set(collapse = TRUE, comment = "#>",
                      message = FALSE, warning = FALSE)
# The pictures of an assembled file are made by data-raw/gen_gallery.R (from
# the Gallery's outputs, through LibreOffice's PDF), committed in
# inst/rtf-examples/assemble/ and copied next to the article to be served.
.here <- normalizePath(".")
.shot <- function(file) {
  src <- file.path(.here, "..", "..", "inst", "rtf-examples", "assemble", file)
  if (!file.exists(src)) return(invisible(NULL))
  dir.create(file.path(.here, "figures", "assemble"), showWarnings = FALSE,
             recursive = TRUE)
  file.copy(src, file.path(.here, "figures", "assemble", file), overwrite = TRUE)
  knitr::include_graphics(file.path("figures", "assemble", file), error = FALSE)
}
```

```{r setup, fold = FALSE}
library(rtfreporter)
```

A clinical deliverable is many tables, listings and figures, each written to
its own `.rtf` by its own program. `assemble_rtf()` joins them into **one
document**: a cover page, a table of contents whose entries are links, each
output starting on its own page with its own running header and footer, and a
bookmark per output, which Word and LibreOffice turn into the PDF's bookmarks.

The Gallery's demographics, adverse events, vital signs and listing, assembled
with a cover page and a table of contents, then converted to PDF with
LibreOffice:

```{r shot-asm-toc, echo = FALSE, fig.alt = "The cover page (Study XYZ-001, Tables and Listings, Draft 1) and the table of contents, with headings and one entry per output; the adverse events entry is boxed in red, with a note that clicking it opens the AE table at page 4 of the PDF."}
.shot("toc.png")
```

Each entry of the table of contents is a link. Click the adverse events entry
and the reader opens that table's first page:

```{r shot-asm-target, echo = FALSE, fig.alt = "Page 4 of the PDF: the first page of Table 14.3.1.1, Treatment-Emergent Adverse Events by SOC and PT."}
.shot("target.png")
```

<details><summary>Show code</summary>

```r
files <- c("t_dm.rtf", "t_ae.rtf", "t_vs.rtf", "l_sae.rtf")   # the Gallery's outputs
assemble_rtf(
  files, "XYZ-001_tables.rtf", overwrite = TRUE,
  cover = list(title = "Study XYZ-001", subtitle = "Tables and Listings",
               version = "Draft 1"),
  toc = data.frame(
    file    = files,
    heading = c("DEMOGRAPHICS", "SAFETY", "SAFETY", "LISTINGS"),
    label   = c("Table 14.1.1  Demographic Characteristics",
                "Table 14.3.1.1  Treatment-Emergent Adverse Events by SOC and PT",
                "Table 14.3.5.1  Vital Signs by Visit",
                "Listing 16.2.7.2  Severe Treatment-Emergent Adverse Events")))
system2("soffice", c("--headless", "--convert-to", "pdf", "XYZ-001_tables.rtf"))
```

</details>

## The outputs first

Each output is written as it always is -- its own program, its own
`generate_rtfreport()`. Here, two small ones:

```{r make-files}
make <- function(title, path) {
  d <- data.frame(A = c("1", "2"), B = c("x", "y"), stringsAsFactors = FALSE)
  doc <- rtf_document() |> rtf_tables(as_rtftables(d), titles = list(c(title)))
  generate_rtfreport(doc, path, overwrite = TRUE); path
}
f1 <- make("Table 14.1.1 Demographics",   tempfile(fileext = ".rtf"))
f2 <- make("Table 14.2.1 Adverse Events",  tempfile(fileext = ".rtf"))
```

## A table of contents from the titles: `toc = "auto"`

`toc = "auto"` builds one TOC entry per file, taking each label from the file's
title: its title rows as the file shows them, joined with two spaces
(`"Table 14.1.1"` and `"Demographics"` give `"Table 14.1.1  Demographics"`):

```{r assemble-auto, fold = "open"}
pkg <- tempfile(fileext = ".rtf")
assemble_rtf(c(f1, f2), pkg, toc = "auto", overwrite = TRUE)
file.exists(pkg)
```

## A cover page and a table of contents of your own: `cover =`, `toc =`

For sections and explicit labels, pass the table of contents as a table: one
row per file, its `label`, and a `heading` printed above the entry whenever it
changes (`level` sets the entry's level; the levels are indented only with
`toc_style = list(indent = )`). Each entry creates an RTF
**bookmark**, so the TOC is navigable in the word processor and the entries jump
to the right table:

```{r assemble-manual, fold = "open"}
pkg2 <- tempfile(fileext = ".rtf")
assemble_rtf(
  c(f1, f2), pkg2,
  cover = list(title = "Study XYZ-001", subtitle = "Final Tables", version = "v1.0"),
  toc = data.frame(
    file    = c(f1, f2),
    heading = c("EFFICACY ANALYSES", "SAFETY ANALYSES"),
    label   = c("Table 14.1.1 Demographics", "Table 14.2.1 Adverse Events")
  ),
  overwrite = TRUE
)
file.exists(pkg2)
```

`assemble_rtf()` also takes a `toc_leader` and a `toc_style` for the table of
contents; see `?assemble_rtf`.

## Page numbers

The assembled document's pages are numbered in one sequence from its first
page: the cover is page 1, the table of contents comes next, then the outputs,
with no restart. The total is all the pages. With a cover, a one-page table of
contents and seven pages of tables, the first table is page 3 of 9 and the
last 9 of 9; the page each entry of the table of contents points to is
counted the same way.

Each output can also keep its own running footer, so a table says *Page 2 of
5* of itself, whichever page of the deliverable it is on: write it with the
static `{PAGE}` / `{TOTAL_PAGES}` tokens, filled in when that output is
written. The dynamic `{AUTO_PAGE}` / `{AUTO_TOTAL_PAGES}` give the
deliverable's own numbers instead, and so does `assemble_rtf(book_page = )`
for a `{BOOK_PAGE}` slot an output reserved.

## Assembling a folder: `assemble_folder()`

To combine every RTF in a directory, `assemble_folder(dir, output_file)` reads
each file's table number and title into a table of contents and assembles them.
Without `output_file` it returns that table instead: edit the order, headings
and labels (or save it with `spec_file =` and edit it in Excel), then pass it
-- or its path -- to `assemble_rtf(toc = )`. See `?assemble_folder`.

## Bookmarks in the PDF, and Word and LibreOffice

The assembled file is RTF. Each table of contents entry is a link to a
bookmark at the start of its file, and each file also starts with a heading
at an outline level, printed invisibly (white, one point high). Word and
LibreOffice show those headings as the PDF's bookmarks when they export the
file to PDF, so the PDF can be navigated table by table, as an eCTD
submission expects. With LibreOffice from R:

```r
system2("soffice", c("--headless", "--convert-to", "pdf", pkg2))
pdftools::pdf_toc(sub("[.]rtf$", ".pdf", pkg2))   # one bookmark a file
```

The page numbers in the table of contents are fields that already hold the
page rtfreporter computed for each file; Word and LibreOffice update them
when they refresh fields. In Word itself a link follows on Ctrl+click, its
default setting.

## Converting to PDF

rtfreporter writes RTF; it does not write PDF. Convert the assembled file to
PDF with Adobe Acrobat or a similar tool -- Word, or LibreOffice -- and keep
the options that create bookmarks from headings.

**A sample.** [`xyz-001-tables-sample.pdf`](../xyz-001-tables-sample.pdf)
(28 pages, 124 KB) is the assembled file above -- the Gallery's outputs, made
from the CDISC pilot data -- converted with **LibreOffice**, not Acrobat.
It opens with the bookmarks panel beside the first page; each bookmark, and
each entry of the table of contents, opens its output's first page:

```{r shot-asm-bookmarks, echo = FALSE, fig.alt = "A PDF viewer drawn from the sample PDF: the Bookmarks panel lists the four outputs (Table 14.1.1, Table 14.3.1.1, Table 14.3.5.1, Listing 16.2.7.2); the adverse events bookmark is selected and page 4 of 28, the first page of that table, is shown beside it."}
.shot("bookmarks.png")
```

The picture is drawn from the sample's own outline and page (by
`data-raw/gen_assemble_pdf.py`); it is not a screenshot of Acrobat.

**With LibreOffice**, the PDF export options that matter are: export
bookmarks, PDF version 1.7 (or PDF/A), initial view "Bookmarks Panel and
Page", default page layout and magnification, lossless images. From the
command line they go in the filter options of `--convert-to`;
`data-raw/gen_assemble_pdf.py` in the package's repository has the full set.

**With Microsoft Word**, as tested with the same kind of file:

- open the RTF, select all (Ctrl+A) and update fields (F9), so the table of
  contents' page numbers and the page fields are current;
- save as PDF with the option that creates bookmarks from headings turned
  on; the PDF/A option is there too, when PDF/A is wanted;
- in Japanese Word, the last empty paragraph can take the East Asian default
  font (for example Yu Mincho), which then appears in the PDF's font list
  (tracked as rtfreporter#1110).

### Optional finishing steps

Two FDA settings can be added after the conversion. Both are optional, and
both use tools outside rtfreporter:

- **Open with the bookmarks panel** (the PDF's `/PageMode /UseOutlines`).
  LibreOffice's "Bookmarks Panel and Page" initial view and Word's export
  already set it; otherwise set the initial view in Acrobat's document
  properties.
- **Fast Web View** (a linearized PDF). LibreOffice and Word's plain export
  do not linearize; Acrobat can, and so can the free command-line tool
  [`qpdf`](https://qpdf.readthedocs.io/):

```sh
qpdf --linearize xyz-001-tables.pdf xyz-001-tables-fwv.pdf
qpdf --check-linearization xyz-001-tables-fwv.pdf
```

The sample had both steps, and its document title and author were set to
neutral values (no person's name).

### The sample against the FDA PDF specifications

Checked against the FDA's *Portable Document Format (PDF) Specifications*,
version 4.1, with `qpdf`, `pypdf` and `PyMuPDF`:

| Item | FDA v4.1 | The sample | Result |
|---|---|---|---|
| PDF version | 1.4 to 1.7, PDF/A-1, PDF/A-2 | 1.7 | Pass |
| Fonts | non-standard fonts fully embedded | Courier New (a standard font), embedded | Pass |
| Security | no security or password | not encrypted | Pass |
| Bookmarks | one for each TOC item | 4 bookmarks, one per output | Pass |
| TOC links | linked TOC; "Inherit Zoom" | 8 links (label and page number), each to its page, zoom inherited | Pass |
| Initial view | Bookmarks Panel and Page; layout and magnification default | `/UseOutlines`, no layout or zoom set | Pass |
| Fast Web View | optimized for fast web view | linearized (`qpdf`) | Pass |
| Page size | 8.5 x 11 in, orientation kept | letter; landscape tables, one portrait | Pass |
| Margins | left 3/4 in; 3/8 in elsewhere; landscape top 3/4 in | every page 0.75 in left and right; top 0.75 in on the table pages, 0.9 in on the cover and TOC | Pass |
| Images | resolution, lossless compression | no images: text only, searchable | Pass |
| JavaScript, external links, attachments | none | none | Pass |
| Metadata | -- | title set, neutral author | Pass |

See `?assemble_rtf` and `?assemble_folder` for every argument.
